# **The PGM Jewellery Monitor** _Covering activity in the Chinese platinum and palladium jewellery manufacturing industry from November 2011 to February 2012_ **David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** **13 April 2012** _April 2012_ ##### **New York:** - Gold is still the most buoyant sector of the Chinese jewellery market with high prices doing little to deter consumers from buying pieces made from the yellow metal. However, platinum demand is rising as retail prices become more competitive and metal prices show a touch more stability than has been seen in recent years. Palladium jewellery demand continues to disappoint. • At a retail level, platinum jewellery generally remains more expensive than gold jewellery, and there is anecdotal evidence that some consumers are concerned about the underlying value of platinum. However, we believe this view is not widespread. More positively, where retailers have been able to reduce platinum prices, they have seen a consumer response, strongly suggesting that customers will buy this metal at the right price. - At a manufacturer level, Chinese output of platinum jewellery rose in the November-February period compared both to the previous four months and to a year earlier. Margins, working stocks and the use of recycled metal changed little, leading us to forecast an increase of roughly ten per cent in net platinum demand from this sector for this calendar year. - The key buying seasons of Chinese New Year and Valentine’s Day saw very strong demand for platinum gem-set jewellery. Retailers built their stocks of plain metal but sales, although more than healthy, evidently disappointed a little compared to the highly optimistic initial forecasts. - Manufacturing volumes of palladium jewellery declined once again. The majority of indicators which we monitor were negative for this sector with margins falling, order books looking less healthy and the use of recycled metal from old, unsold stocks of palladium jewellery rising. 200 Park Avenue, New York, NY 10166 0130 Tel: +1 212 878 4122 ##### **London:** 4th Floor, St Martins Court, 10 Paternoster Row, London EC4M 7BB Tel: +44 20 7489 6767 ##### **Hong Kong:** Suite 1306, Two Exchange Square, 8 Connaught Place, Central, Hong Kong Tel: +852 2899 2026 ##### **Tokyo:** 2-1 Ohtemachi 1-Chome, Chiyoda-Ku, Tokyo 100 Tel: +81 33 285 3407 ##### **Singapore:** 80 Robinson Road, #15-02, Singapore, 068898 Tel: +65 6372 8050 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | The PGM Jewellery Monitor** **13 April 2012** ## **Platinum** Manufacturing volumes Forecast volumes Optimism Pt:Pd ratio

Chinese platinum jewellery manufacturing volumes increased in the November to February period compared to one year earlier. Although output in the July to October timeframe is always boosted by October’s National Day holidays, the early part of 2012 contained two key buying occasions, Chinese New Year and Valentine’s Day, and production was therefore higher than it had been in the previous four months too. There were some signs of strong consumer demand, particularly for gem-set platinum jewellery but there were also indications that there had been some over-ordering of platinum stock by retailers and wholesalers, leading to disappointing levels of new orders in late February and early March. In the short term, the jewellery manufacturers generally remain optimistic for platinum’s prospects, with retail demand seemingly robust. However, we have heard comments that some consumers at least are aware of the narrow differential between platinum and gold in terms of the raw metal price and are therefore sceptical over platinum’s real value. We believe, however, that this is not a widespread sentiment amongst the general public. Of greater concern to us is the increasing interest being shown by companies which we would normally consider _platinum_ jewellery manufacturing companies in producing yellow gold pieces. Turnover of gold remains substantially faster than platinum jewellery turnover and although gold jewellery production poses different technical challenges to platinum production, it will compete for some of the same resources. _High figures indicate an increase in a measure and low figures indicate a decrease in a measure. 5 indicates no change from the last reporting period. Pt:Pd ratio compares the amount of each metal used by manufacturers with a high figure showing platinum taking market share from palladium._ The number of employees at the platinum manufacturers has changed little over the last few months and working stocks are little different to their levels in late 2011, both factors signifying that demand is not racing too far ahead of last year’s level. Nonetheless, we feel that demand for fresh platinum looks set to rise by between five and ten per cent this year, with the manufacturers largely optimistic. (We note, though, very strong recent physical buying interest which could be an additional positive sign of stronger demand.) Looking at our other indicators, margins have been maintained at a healthy level, suggesting that platinum remains an attractive product to manufacture but that no new entrants have appeared in this market. The use of recycled metal from old or unsold jewellery has changed little during the last year and, unless metal prices rise, we expect changes in retail demand to be reflected in changes in manufacturer purchases of new metal. 2

The health of the palladium jewellery market continues to worsen. While there are still pockets of good retail demand within China (in Guangdong, Henan, Shandong and Szechuan provinces), sales are evidently much less strong than before, with demand in the North-East of the country, where we had previously seen large quantities of palladium on sale, decreasing. This is reflected in our figure for manufacturing volumes (above) which continue to show a substantial year-on-year fall. This is confirmed by lower working stocks of palladium (implying less throughput of material) and in lower finished stocks (implying less wholesaler and retailer demand). _High figures indicate an increase in a measure and low figures indicate a decrease in a measure. 5 indicates no change from the last reporting period._ Manufacturer forecasts are for a further decline in palladium demand, although the rate of decline is expected to be lower than it has been in the last year or so. In our view, this is not related to the quality of palladium jewellery produced but rather to limited consumer awareness of palladium as a brand and movements in the bare metal price. More worrying for the state of the market is that margins on palladium jewellery have fallen once again. Looking back several years, there were considerably more palladium jewellery manufacturers active than is the case today. A shrinking market has encouraged many to end palladium production in favour of platinum, white gold or yellow gold. However, even with fewer manufacturers currently involved, there is still pressure on margins, suggesting that there is excess capacity. The use of recycled metal has also increased by a reasonable amount in the last year, with most of this coming from stocks of unsold jewellery, suggesting that consumer demand is still rather weak. 3

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | The PGM Jewellery Monitor** **13 April 2012** ## **Notes to methodology** This survey uses similar methodology to previous reports issued by Mitsui Precious Metals on the gold refining market. Mitsui surveys a large number of participants in the Chinese jewellery market to obtain semi-quantitative information on the market. This data is then weighted by the importance of the respondent and averaged across the industry. High figures indicate an increase in the measure and low figures indicate a decrease in a measure. 5 indicates no change from the last reporting period. The survey does not aim to report on changes in consumer behaviour except in an anecdotal sense but rather to add some further detail to the qualitative understanding of demand for metal at the major jewellery manufacturers within China. For quantitative figures on demand, we refer the reader to the usual Johnson Matthey and GFMS reports on the platinum group metal market. ## **Timescale** This survey covers manufacturing and other activity from November 2011 to the end of February 2012 inclusive, a period which includes the Chinese New Year and Valentine’s Day. Forward-looking production forecasts relate to the next four month period while optimism measures longer term views. Backward-looking data is compared to the same period one year earlier. ## **Terminology** In any report on a technical subject, the use of technical terms is unavoidable so we list here definitions of as many of these terms as possible: |950, 990, 999
